summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework sets what a trans visitor faces at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows federal procedure. Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and trigger secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request alternative screening and may decline the scanner. The agency's own know-your-rights guidance covers U.S. nationals travelling to and from the territory on the same terms as mainland travellers, including what may and may not be carried in hand baggage under the federal screening framework.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

Territorial law provides an additional layer of protection. The U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending the protection explicitly into the education setting.

Relationship and marital status are settled. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide; a married couple can rely on their marriage in the territory. The historic sodomy statute applied to the territory since 1957 has been replaced and is no longer in force.
tangentialFactors:
Two legal layers operate simultaneously in the territory: federal rules that control documents, border screening and federal funding, and territorial statutes that govern discrimination claims, marriage and local services. Protection against discrimination in a hotel, restaurant or shop therefore rests on territorial law, while the documents a visitor carries and the screening they undergo at entry rest on federal law.

The March 2017 Attorney General's interpretation applied an existing statute rather than creating a new one, which means the underlying protection had been on the books before that ruling and continues after it. The scope of that protection beyond the education setting is set by the statute's own terms, which the sources reviewed here do not reproduce in full.

The 2015 Superior Court ruling on marriage predated the nationwide position and was subsequently reinforced by federal recognition, so the territory is not an outlier on this question and same-sex couples should not expect a different treatment there than elsewhere under United States jurisdiction.

Local reporting from 2017 describes both setbacks and continued advocacy for the LGBTQ community in the territory, indicating an active but contested local politics around these protections rather than a settled consensus.
localsOnly:
Residents of the U.S. Virgin Islands are covered by the territorial human-rights law, which prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. The Attorney General's March 2017 interpretation confirmed that this coverage extends to transgender students, giving residents and families a documented official position to cite in school settings.

Residents hold United States documents and are subject to the same federal document rules as other United States nationals, including the sex-marker policy applied since January 2025. Changing the marker on a resident's passport follows national procedure, not territorial procedure.

Residents at federally funded institutions in the territory fall within the January 2025 executive order on gender-affirming care funding, so coverage and provision at those institutions is affected in the same way as on the mainland.

Marriage for same-sex couples has been lawful in the territory since the 2015 Superior Court ruling, and residents' marriages are federally recognised.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the U.S. Virgin Islands issues any territorial identity or driver-licence document carrying a gender marker that differs from the federal standard is not sourced here and remains unresolved; the sources reviewed address federal passports only.

The enforcement record of the territorial anti-discrimination law, including how complaints by transgender residents and visitors have been handled since the 2017 Attorney General interpretation, is not documented in the sources reviewed and remains unresolved.

Territorial health-insurance and Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care, separate from the federal funding restrictions, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The practical implementation of the January 2025 federal funding order at named institutions in the territory, and whether any territorial programme fills resulting gaps, is not documented in the sources reviewed and remains unresolved.

The current wording of the territorial sodomy statute as replaced, and whether consent-in-private conduct is fully protected, is not reproduced in the sources reviewed and remains unresolved.
